title: ALCOA+ Principles — The Foundation of Data Integrity
summary: ALCOA+ is the universally accepted framework for data integrity in regulated industries. Every computerized system handling GxP data must satisfy these principles. ALCOA+ applies to both electronic and paper records.

A — Attributable.requirement: Every action on a record must be traceable to the person who performed it
system_implications: Unique user accounts — no shared or generic accounts (e.g., no 'admin', 'lab1', 'rep_team')
User authentication before any data creation or modification
Audit trail captures user identity with every action
Electronic signatures identify the signer by name
API and integration actions must be traceable to the initiating user or system
common_violations: Shared login accounts in production systems
Service accounts performing actions on behalf of users without recording the original user
Audit trail shows system user ID instead of human user for batch operations
Mobile devices shared between field reps without proper session management

L — Legible.requirement: Data must be readable, permanent, and unambiguous throughout its retention period
system_implications: Records must be displayable in human-readable format
Exports must produce complete and accurate copies
Data must survive platform migrations without loss of readability
PDF/CSV exports must include all relevant fields including audit trail data
Encrypted data must be decryptable when needed for regulatory review
common_violations: Encoded or serialized data stored without a documented decoding mechanism
Historical records become unreadable after system migration
Exported reports truncate long fields or omit audit trail entries
Signature images degrade in quality during migration

C — Contemporaneous.requirement: Data must be recorded at the time the activity occurs, not after the fact
system_implications: System timestamps must reflect actual event time, not data entry time
Mobile offline data must preserve the original capture timestamp, not the sync timestamp
Backdating of records must be prevented or flagged in the audit trail
Time zone handling must be correct and documented
Server clocks must be synchronized via NTP
common_violations: Mobile CRM records showing sync timestamp instead of visit/activity timestamp
Batch data loads that stamp all records with the load timestamp
Users allowed to freely modify date/time fields on historical records
Time zone confusion causing apparent backdating (UTC vs local time)

O — Original.requirement: The first recording of data is the original record. Subsequent copies are certified true copies only if verified as exact and complete.
system_implications: Electronic records in the system of record are the 'original' — not printouts
If data originates in one system and flows to another, the source system holds the original
Certified true copies (for regulatory submissions) must include all fields, audit trail, and metadata
Data migration must produce validated true copies with documented verification
common_violations: Organizations claiming paper printouts are the 'official' record while the electronic record is the true original
Data migration without verification that migrated records match source records exactly
Deleting source system records after migration without proper archive

A — Accurate.requirement: Data must be correct, truthful, and free from errors. Corrections must not obscure the original entry.
system_implications: Validation rules to prevent obviously incorrect data entry
Audit trail preserves original values when records are corrected
Deleted records are soft-deleted (marked inactive) not hard-deleted
Calculations and derived values must be verified and reproducible
Integration data must be validated at receipt — not blindly trusted
common_violations: Hard deletion of records without audit trail
Overwriting field values without capturing the previous value
Allowing administrators to directly modify database records bypassing the application layer
Batch updates that overwrite corrected values with stale data from source systems

Complete (+ extension).requirement: All data must be present — including retests, OOS results, outliers, and failed attempts. No selective reporting.
system_implications: System must not allow selective deletion of unfavorable results
Voided or cancelled records must be retained with reason codes
Retry/re-test attempts must all be captured, not just the successful one
Reporting must include all records, not just filtered subsets

Consistent (+ extension).requirement: Data must be recorded in a consistent, chronologically logical sequence. Timestamps should make sense in context.
system_implications: Workflow enforcement to prevent out-of-sequence operations
Timestamps should show logical progression (visit start < sample drop < signature < visit end)
System should flag chronological anomalies (e.g., signature timestamp before visit start)

Enduring (+ extension).requirement: Data must be recorded on permanent media, not temporary storage that could be lost.
system_implications: Data must not reside solely in volatile storage (session cache, local storage without sync)
Mobile offline data must be designed to survive app crashes and device reboots
Export files for regulatory submissions must be in durable formats (PDF/A, CSV)

Available (+ extension).requirement: Data must be accessible for review and inspection throughout its required retention period.
system_implications: Archived data must remain queryable and retrievable
System retirement must include data accessibility plan
Data must be available to regulatory inspectors upon request — typically within 24-48 hours
Retention periods vary: 3 years (PDMA samples), 15 years (clinical trial data), life of product + 2 years (adverse events)

title: Data Integrity Regulatory Enforcement — Warning Letters and Trends
summary: Data integrity has been the #1 FDA enforcement topic since 2015. Understanding enforcement trends helps organizations prioritize their validation efforts.
enforcement_trends: FDA issued 30+ Warning Letters citing data integrity violations from 2015-2024
MHRA (UK) has been the most aggressive EU regulator on data integrity — multiple site closures
PMDA (Japan) made data integrity the primary focus of GMP inspections starting 2015
WHO published comprehensive data integrity guidance in 2016 (TRS 996 Annex 5)
Most Warning Letters involve: shared accounts, missing audit trails, backdated records, and deleted unfavorable results
common_findings_in_inspections: Shared user accounts — the single most common Part 11 finding
Insufficient audit trail — either not enabled or not reviewing audit trail data
No periodic review — systems validated once and never re-evaluated
Inadequate change control — changes to validated systems without impact assessment
Insufficient vendor management — no vendor audit for cloud/SaaS providers
Training gaps — users not trained on electronic record/signature responsibilities
Data deletion — records hard-deleted without audit trail or justification
Insufficient backup/restore testing — backups exist but never tested
inspection_readiness_checklist: Can you demonstrate unique user accounts for all system users?
Can you show an immutable audit trail for any GxP record?
Can you produce a Validation Summary Report for this system?
Can you show the most recent periodic review report?
Can you demonstrate your change control process for this system?
Can you show vendor qualification documentation?
Can you produce training records for all current users?
Can you demonstrate backup/restore by performing a test restore?
Can you produce records in both electronic and human-readable format?
Can you show your validation traceability matrix with full test coverage?

title: Audit Trail Configuration Best Practices for Cloud/SaaS Platforms
summary: Platform-native audit trail capabilities vary widely. Understanding the gaps and remediation options is critical for Part 11 and Annex 11 compliance.

what_must_be_captured: WHO — user identity (not just user ID, but resolvable to a named person)
WHAT — field-level old value and new value
WHY — reason for change (for high-risk fields; may require a custom 'reason for change' prompt)
Record creation (including which user created it and when)
Record deletion or inactivation (soft delete preferred)
Login/logout events and failed login attempts
common_platform_gaps: Field history tracking limited to N fields per object (Salesforce: 20 fields)
Audit trail retention shorter than regulatory requirement (Salesforce Setup Audit Trail: 180 days)
No native 'reason for change' capture — must be custom-built
Deleted records may not retain full audit history
Bulk data operations may bypass field-level audit trail
API-initiated changes may not capture the originating user consistently
Formula fields and rollup summaries are calculated, not audited
remediation_approaches: Custom audit trail objects — trigger-based capture of all field changes with no field count limit
Event-driven audit capture — platform events or change data capture for real-time audit logging
Third-party audit trail solutions (e.g., Salesforce Shield, Odaseva, OwnBackup)
External audit log aggregation (Splunk, ELK) for long-term retention
Custom 'reason for change' lightning components for high-risk fields
Soft-delete patterns with IsDeleted flags and RecycleBin retention
